chapter: Mutes, influences and the blues singers
title: His theory of how jazz began, and clapping on the wrong beat
summary: He thinks jazz came out of communal singing and gospel feeling that cannot be taught, and objects to a TV singer clapping the wrong beat.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Another reason I'm glad you asked me that. Let me mention this. To my mind -- I've had a lot of people come up, I've heard them ask others, how was jazz started? Who started jazz? Who was the first to do this? To my mind that was it, because back -- the same thing, back in the time of the same thing up there, it happened to all the people together, singing, shaking hands, praying, with all those gospel songs, other religious songs, that's how it came about, I think. Now, that's the way I think.

Because it gave it the feeling that you can't study, you can't pay a teacher a million dollars to teach you that feeling. Give me that feeling. How the -- I was looking at a program last night. I won't call the name, but they were doing the best that they could, and now the thing was swinging. But this particular person, who's been in the business for 50 years, she did the best she could do. She was -- she was clapping her hand on the beat, Hah (clap), hah (clap), hah (clap) Hah (clap) hah (clap), you know. But I mean that's not the way. And when you're doing jazz, but what are you
going to do about it? That's the way she felt it, and that's the way I've known -- that's thousands, and maybe millions of people feel that beat, but that's not it.
It's the (snap) instead of the (snap) (snap) (snap), you know.
Yeah, I mean that's the way they feel, and they -- they don't know. Let's get hot! Jah, jah, jah, hah, hah, hah, you know.
